title: streaming-sse-chunking-backpressure-debug-notes
content:
Summary:
Quick scratchpad for repro + breadcrumbs for the intermittent streaming bug we're seeing in hosted API: clients occasionally stop receiving SSE chunks mid-stream or receive very long pauses (~10s+) between chunks, causing downstream backpressure and timeouts. Observed across Node fetch clients and our Python long-poll consumer. Repro steps + commands below.

Background / symptoms:
- A subset of requests to /v1/streams/generate (SSE) yield either:
  - long pauses between SSE events (~5-30s) even though server shows tokens being generated on GPU, or
  - client sees only a partial final event (no terminating [DONE] event), stream stalls, connection remains open until client times out.
- Client-side effects: event queue growth, memory spikes in some clients, request-level timeouts and retries.
- Server-side: logs for the request show continuous token generation; runtime metrics (gpu_util, kernel time) look fine. No obvious OOM.
- Happens more often under moderate load (50-200 concurrent streaming requests).

Minimal repro (local):
1) Start a minimal server that proxies a streaming response and intentionally chunks output (simulates runtime chunking). Use the following Python server snippet (uvicorn + FastAPI):

# server.py (local repro)
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
import asyncio

app = FastAPI()

async def slow_stream():
    for i in range(60):
        # emulate token produced every ~100ms but sent in variable chunk sizes
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1 if i % 10 != 0 else 1.2)
        yield f"data: {i}\n\n"

    # final done event
    yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"

@app.get('/proxy-stream')
async def proxy():
    return StreamingResponse(slow_stream(), media_type='text/event-stream')

# run: uvicorn server:app --port 8080

2) Curl client repro (observes pauses):
curl -N http://localhost:8080/proxy-stream | sed -u 's/^/RECV: /'

3) Node fetch SSE client (minimal):
const fetch = require('node-fetch');
(async () => {
  const res = await fetch('http://localhost:8080/proxy-stream');
  res.body.on('data', chunk => console.log('chunk:', chunk.toString()));
})();

Observed behavior for the local repro:
- curl prints bursts of events then long pause at predictable points (every 10 tokens in my slow_stream).
- Node fetch receives chunks that sometimes aggregate multiple events (ok) and sometimes split in the middle of an event (bad) — leads to parser code failing if it assumes event delimiter boundaries.

Real incident reproduction against staging (what I ran):
- Request (curl) to staging streaming endpoint with streaming=true + chunked transfer enabled:
curl -N -v -H 'Authorization: Bearer XXXX' \
  -H 'Accept: text/event-stream' \
  -d '{"prompt":"<long prompt>","stream":true}' \
  https://staging-api.redwood-inference.internal/v1/streams/generate

- Terminal snippet (truncated):
* Connected to staging-api...
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
< Content-Type: text/event-stream; charset=utf-8
< Transfer-Encoding: chunked

data: {"token":"Hello"}\n\n
data: {"token":" world"}\n\n\n
data: {"token":"!"}\n\n\n# THEN LONG PAUSE (~18s)
# then a final block that appears as a single big chunk:

data: {"token":"rest-of-output..."}\n
data: [DONE]\n\n- Client-side logs (Node) during incident: many small data events, then large gap, then a large "data" chunk containing many concatenated tokens.

Server logs around the time (sanitized):
- request_id=abc123: started inference on model redwood-mosaic
- request_id=abc123: token_generated index=35 latency_ms=18 kernel_ms=10
- request_id=abc123: token_generated index=36 latency_ms=17
- ... tokens continue generating at ~10-25ms per token
- request_id=abc123: finished inference, total_tokens=240
- request_id=abc123: stream flush initiated

Hypotheses (brainstorm):
- Nagle-like aggregation at some TCP layer (but we use keepalive and small writes). Under some conditions kernel writes may be aggregated by OS/TCP stack into fewer larger packets, causing long pauses between visible chunks.
- Proxy (ingress Nginx / Envoy) performing buffering for chunked responses — maybe enabled for some content-length/headers combos.
- Our streaming runtime does variable write patterns: sometimes writes small writes per token, sometimes batches several tokens and flushes; mismatch with proxy keep-alive/flush settings could create pauses.
- Backpressure on the socket: if client isn't reading rapidly, kernel send buffers fill causing writes to block in runtime; runtime then delays flushing to avoid blocking threads. But server logs show token generation continued, so downstream flush might be deferred until buffer pressure clears (would explain large final chunk).
- HTTP/2 vs HTTP/1.1: behavior differs by client/proxy; staging runs h2 between front proxy and runtime? Need to confirm.

Things I tried (commands + results):
- Added explicit flush on runtime after each token write (write + syscall "fsync" style) — mitigated in local repro but not fully in staging.
- Disabled proxy buffering in a local Envoy config (set buffer limits to 0 / enable chunked streaming) — behavior improved locally.
- Experimented with curl --no-buffer / -N — allowed seeing bytes immediately in local repro.
- Set TCP_NODELAY on server sockets — helped reduce aggregation on local reproduction. Need to validate on staging.
- Increased server-side write timeout and decreased proxy downstream buffering timeouts to force more immediate flushes. Mixed results.

Debug artifacts / logs attached (where to look):
- ingress (envoy/nginx) logs around request_id=abc123 — check for proxied_downstream_flush, buffer_full events.
- kernel tcp_info for socket (ss -ti) while reproducing — look for snd_cwnd, unacked, rtt.
- runtime logs: toggled debug chunking logs (added log lines every 10ms write) — compare to kernel send timing.
- client traces: Node process dump showing event loop activity during long pauses.

Immediate next steps (plan):
- Add a gated reproduction on staging with direct-to-runtime bypassing ingress (if possible) to determine whether ingress is the culprit. If bypass shows no pauses, root cause likely proxy buffering.
- Add small instrumentation: timestamp (ms) appended to each token payload for a few experiments so we can measure server-write -> client-receive delta precisely. E.g., data: {"token":"x","ts_write":167...}
- Run a load test that mimics production concurrency (50-200 concurrent streaming reqs) with direct-to-runtime and with ingress to compare. Use vegeta or a custom Node runner that parses SSE.
- If ingress implicated, try changing Envoy config: set 'use_remote_address', enable immediate flush (http2_stream_idle_timeout?), disable response_buffering for the route, and set buffer limits small.
- If kernel level: ensure TCP_NODELAY is set, and experiment with smaller send buffer sizes on runtime side to avoid large aggregations.

Notes to self / open questions:
- Which versions of Envoy/NGINX are deployed in staging? Are there known bugs with streaming chunk flush? (Kyla to confirm).
- Do we have HTTP/2 between front proxy and runtime worker? That would change semantics (frames vs chunked).
- Are customers using proxies that may re-buffer (e.g., Cloudflare, API gateway)? Could be customer-side too.

Quick TODOs:
- [ ] Add ts_write to token payload (quick flag-guarded change)
- [ ] Repro with direct-to-runtime on staging (ask infra for short-lived bypass)
- [ ] Run comparative load test (direct vs via ingress) and collect p95 inter-chunk latency
- [ ] If ingress implicated, test Envoy config tweaks in staging canary
- [ ] If kernel/stack implicated, try TCP_NODELAY + tune send buffer sizes in runtime

Appendix: useful commands and snippets
- Check open sockets and tcp_info for pid 1234:
sudo ss -ti -K dst 10.1.2.3
- Curl with no buffering + verbose:
curl -N -v -H 'Accept: text/event-stream' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -d '{"stream":true}' https://staging-api.redwood-inference.internal/v1/streams/generate
- Simple Node SSE parser (for load testing):
const http = require('http');
const fetch = require('node-fetch');
(async function() {
  const r = await fetch(process.argv[2]);
  r.body.on('data', d => process.stdout.write('.'))
})();
- Small vegeta style load runner (script in python) to spawn many clients and log per-event timings (I put a draft in /tmp/vegeta-streamer.py)

If anyone picks this up: start by running the local repro (server.py) and test against a variety of client readers (curl, node-fetch, our python client) — this usually reproduces the parsing-edge-case and chunk boundaries. For production-grade pauses we need the direct-to-runtime staging test to disambiguate proxy vs runtime.

End of notes.
